blindSummary:
This country is among the most legally protective jurisdictions in its region for trans visitors. Since 2022, anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes are criminal offences covering SOGI explicitly; the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover sexual orientation and gender identity; and a pride march in the capital goes through the city centre under police protection. The country's candidacy for membership in a neighbouring economic-political bloc is driving continued legal alignment.

Counterweights: there is still no accessible legal gender recognition (a medicalised process exists on paper but the leading national LGBT+ organisation reports it is not functional in practice), the dominant national church and major politicians (including the capital's mayor) regularly issue homophobic statements, and a breakaway region occupied by a foreign power has its own anti-LGBT "propaganda" law — travellers should treat that region as a separate, much riskier jurisdiction.
blindOutOfScope: The breakaway region is scored as part of this country de jure, but travellers should treat it separately: it is under foreign military occupation, has an anti-LGBT propaganda law, and there is no consular access. General poverty and corruption affect all travellers.
blindSourceSummaries: Regional LGBTI-rights organisation annual review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on this country: a trans woman was denied service at a bank due to document/appearance mismatch - the national equality body confirmed discrimination; hate speech by politicians increased during election campaigns (one parliamentary party's newspaper called for a 'ban on gay parades and LGBT propaganda in schools'); the location of a national trans organisation's camp was disclosed online, forcing relocation; hate crimes and domestic violence reported; civil society helped LGBT+ people fleeing the war in a neighbouring country.

Report (2025) by the national section of an international human-rights organisation: discrimination against LGBTI people remained commonplace; freedom of expression and assembly arbitrarily restricted; in the occupied breakaway region new legislation prohibits what authorities call the promotion of 'non-traditional' sexual relations.

Leading national LGBT+ organisation's report on the situation of LGBT+ rights here (2023): the national equality body's 2022 study found extremely low acceptance - 79% of the population would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% not as work colleagues; social distance score 5.7; marginalisation of LGBT+ people increased in 2022 amid pandemic, economic and security crises.

LGBTQ magazine (Feb 2026): revisits this country's 2024 pride march - a country slowly emerging from its past to carve a new queer identity; participants of all ages and backgrounds join the festivities.

Regional equality-body legislative analysis related to SOGI and HIV in this country (2024): identifies legal barriers affecting the quality of life of LGBT people and people living with HIV, based on a survey completed by local partners.

A foreign government's 2006 human-rights report for this country: documents police beatings, harsh prisons, societal violence and discrimination - baseline assessment including the situation of sexual minorities.

LGBTQ news outlet (May 2018): police fired tear gas at anti-LGBT protesters to protect a pride march in the capital; 20 embassies signed a statement of support for the march; the head of state at the time had publicly attacked the event the previous year.

LGBTQ news outlet (March 2013): a court of appeal in the country's second city struck down that city's 'homosexual propaganda' ban as unconstitutional and a human-rights violation, also criticising the same city's declaration of a 'zone of enhanced support for the national church' - both issued after church-led protests against the bloc-backed anti-discrimination law.
blindLocalsOnly: The non-functional legal gender recognition process is resident-facing.
